prime.problem: To find the median or the 95th percentile you don't need the whole order, yet sorting pays n log n for all of it. The question is how to use a partition to discard most of the data without losing the answer.
prime.fits: Right after quicksort, and built from its partition. The only change is recursing into one side instead of two, which divide and conquer later shows is the difference between n log n and n.
prime.goal: Trace quickselect on a small array, explain why it's linear on average but quadratic in the worst case, and pick it over sorting or a heap for the right queries.

attend: After one partition, how do you know which side holds the k-th smallest, and how does k change when you go right?
Why does throwing one side away turn quicksort's n per level into a shrinking geometric series?
Why does the random-pivot expectation land near 3.39n rather than the 2n of perfect halving?
What goes wrong with the source's arr[0] pivot and recursion on range(1000)?
Why does a separate "equal" group make [5] × 1,000 finish in one level?

must: Partition around p → p's rank among the items is known → k falls left, in the equal block, or right → recurse into one side only (k − n when going right) → the other side is discarded for good

Only the surviving side is scanned next → sizes n, ≈ n/2, ≈ n/4 … → total ≈ 2n with perfect halving, ≤ 2(1 + ln 2)n ≈ 3.39n expected with random pivots → O(n), versus quicksort's n per level for log n levels
A fixed pivot on sorted input keeps only one item off each level → n(n − 1)/2 (21 on sorted a, k = 7) → random pivot in practice, or median of medians / introselect for a worst-case O(n) guarantee
elevated: Three-way split puts all copies of p in the middle → duplicates end in one level (999 compares for [5] × 1,000 vs 499,500 with a two-way split)

compress.prompt: In 3–4 sentences from memory: how quickselect decides which side to keep and how it updates k, why that makes it O(n) on average, and what forces its worst case and what prevents it.
checklist: partition once around a pivot, like quicksort
k ≤ |smaller| → left; k > |≤ p| → right with k minus that count; else p is the answer
only one side survives, so work is n + n/2 + … ≈ constant × n
a bad fixed pivot (arr[0] on sorted input) gives n(n − 1)/2
random pivot, or introselect / median of medians for a guarantee

retrieve.q: Explain why quickselect is O(n) on average while quicksort, built on the same partition, is O(n log n).
answer: quicksort recurses into both sides, so every level still costs about n, for about log n levels
quickselect keeps one side, so each level costs a constant fraction of the one before
the geometric series sums to a constant × n

retrieve.q: Trace the card's level 3 on [3, 9, 10] with k = 3 and pivot 3: what are smaller and larger, what is the rule's test, and what are the new list and k?
A dashboard needs the 50th, 90th and 99th percentiles of the same 10⁶ latencies every minute. Quickselect three times, sort once, or a heap? Justify with costs.
answer: three quickselects: ≈ 3 × O(n) expected, with no guarantee against a bad pivot
sort once (O(n log n)), then every rank is an O(1) index, and more ranks are free
a size-k heap is O(n log k) and good for k small, but the median has k = n/2
for a few ranks either works; many ranks or repeated queries favour sorting

compare.q: Both find a median. Median of two arrays runs in O(log min(m, n)) and quickselect in expected O(n). Which assumption buys the log, and what does each do when it isn't true?
answer: the cut search needs both arrays already sorted; it only moves a boundary
quickselect needs no order at all; it discovers ranks by partitioning
on unsorted data the cut trick doesn't apply, and sorting first costs n log n, so quickselect wins
on sorted data quickselect wastes its O(n) rediscovering what the order already tells you

compare.q: heapq.nsmallest(k, a) vs quickselect for the k-th smallest: what does each keep in memory, what does each cost, and when does the heap win?
answer: the heap keeps k items and pays log k per element: O(n log k)
quickselect keeps the surviving side and pays expected O(n) for any k
the heap wins for small k or streaming data you can't hold; at k = n/2 it's no better than sorting

predict.q: On a = [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] with the source's arr[0] pivot, which k finishes fastest, and how many compares does it take? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: k = 5, in 6 compares: the first pivot is 38, which has 4 smaller items and nothing equal, so its rank is exactly 5 and it is the answer after one level. By contrast k = 1 needs 11 compares and k = 7 needs 7. Cost depends on how fast the pivots' ranks close in on k, not on k's size.

apply.task: Run the card's rule by hand with pivot = arr[0] on a for k = 2 and for k = 6. At each level write the list, the pivot, smaller / larger and the new k, and count one compare per non-pivot item. Then compare with the card's worst case (sorted input, k = 7).
apply.done: k = 2 → 9 in 12 compares over four levels (pivots 38, 27, 3, 9); k = 6 → 43 in 7 compares over two levels; both below the 21 of the sorted-input worst case.
apply.hint: For k = 6 the first level keeps [43, 82] with k = 6 − 5 = 1.
